name: Dyckman Farmhouse

dates.note: The Library's item line dates the structure 'ca. 1783'. The survey's own narrative says William Dyckman returned to Kingsbridge in 1783, found the earlier house burnt, and 'proceeded at once to build the present house on its new site' -- which reads as 1783 or just after. Both kept.
dates.altered: The survey: 'The house had two extensions ... The one to the north was relatively new, dating about 1830 ... This has now been removed.' It also describes the house 'as restored in 1918 and since then preserved'.

quotes.text: "The house itself has basement, parlor floor, bedroom floor and attic. It is "well built. Its stone walls are twenty inches thick, and are con-tinued up to the window ledges of the sleeping-room floor; above them, heavy, hand-hewn white oak beams covered with wide clapboards fill in the space to the peak of the gambrel roof, which, incidentally, has an exceptionally graceful curve.

measurements.note: NO VALUE IS RECORDED. The survey names four levels; both nodes describe this house as a fieldstone lower storey with a frame storey above under the gambrel, which is a reading of the same fabric, not a count the survey made.

note: Tranche 2, the Dutch trunk in America. The quoted 1917 description does in one sentence what both nodes' prose does at length: the stone wall stops at the upper window sills, and above it a light frame fills out to the gambrel -- masonry only where masonry earns its cost. It also records the sprung curve directly, 'the gambrel roof, which, incidentally, has an exceptionally graceful curve', which is the nearest thing in this cluster's surveys to a statement of the spring eave. The 20-inch wall is at the bottom of `hudson-valley-dutch`'s stated 20-30 in band, matching the Abraham Hasbrouck measurement.
